docs.title: Ideas in Economics (Doing Economics)
docs.text:
A film-based introduction to economic thinking | FLAME University | 2 Credits | Level 100

Economics is a way of understanding the world. This course uses six films as a gateway to fundamental economic ideas, pairing each with a Nobel Prize-winning contribution that shaped how economists think about markets, behavior, poverty, growth, and the environment.

No prior knowledge of economics is required. By the end of this course, you will have developed a strong grasp of economic reasoning and its applications to everyday life, policy, and the Indian economy.

docs.title: Module 1: Understanding Economic Thinking
docs.text:
The Big Short (2015) Richard Thaler

Scarcity, opportunity cost, trade-offs, market bubbles, and the clash between rational and behavioral decision-making. Why do financial crises happen, and what does it mean to think like an economist?

Start Module 1

docs.title: Module 2: Incentives and Human Behavior
docs.text:
A Beautiful Mind (2001) John Nash

Game theory, strategic interactions, cooperation vs. competition, and how incentive structures shape human behavior. What happens when every individual acts in their own interest?

Start Module 2

docs.title: Module 3: Market Dynamics and Labor Markets
docs.text:
Margin Call (2011) Paul Krugman

Supply, demand, equilibrium, market failures, labor markets, and globalization. How do prices coordinate millions of decisions, and what happens when markets break down?

Start Module 3

docs.title: Module 4: Poverty, Inequality, and Development
docs.text:
Slumdog Millionaire (2008) Esther Duflo & Abhijit Banerjee

Measuring poverty, informal economies, livelihood strategies, and evidence-based approaches to development. What actually works in lifting people out of poverty?

Start Module 4

docs.title: Module 5: Innovation, Technology, and Growth
docs.text:
Moneyball (2011) Robert Solow

Innovation, productivity, data-driven decision-making, and the economics of long-term growth. What drives economies forward, and how do new ideas displace old ones?

Start Module 5

docs.title: Module 6: Environmental and Public Economics
docs.text:
Erin Brockovich (2000) Elinor Ostrom

Externalities, public goods, common resources, and sustainability. When markets fail to protect the environment, what can communities, governments, and institutions do?

Start Module 6

docs.title: Course Features
docs.text: Feature Description Film Analysis Each module anchors on a feature film, with scene-by-scene economic deconstruction Nobel Focus Biographical profiles of laureates whose work illuminates each module's theme :india: Indian Context Dedicated essays connecting economic concepts to the Indian economy Interactive Sims 30+ browser-based simulations from the Introduction to Economics open textbook Quizzes 10-question self-assessment per module with explanations Glossary 120+ terms defined with examples

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
1. Begin with Module 1: Understanding Economic Thinking
  2. Watch the assigned film before or alongside the module reading
  3. Explore the interactive simulations linked in each module
  4. Test yourself with the end-of-module quiz
  5. Read the Indian Context essays for local applications

Prepared by Ravikiran Naik, FLAME University

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
Economics is a way of understanding the world. This course uses films as a gateway to introduce fundamental economic concepts. Through movie analysis and Nobel Prize-winning research, students explore market behavior, incentives, labor dynamics, development, and policy. The course also serves as a foundation for further study in microeconomics and macroeconomics.

No prior knowledge of economics is required. By engaging with stories told on screen and the ideas of some of the greatest economic thinkers, students develop an intuition for how economic reasoning applies to everyday life, public policy, and the Indian economy.

docs.title: Course Objectives
docs.text:
1. Introduce core economic concepts through accessible, real-world narratives drawn from cinema, enabling students to connect abstract ideas to concrete situations.
  2. Develop economic reasoning skills by analyzing trade-offs, incentives, market behavior, and strategic interactions as depicted in feature films.
  3. Expose students to landmark economic research by pairing each module with the work of a Nobel Prize-winning economist, grounding film-based discussions in rigorous scholarship.
  4. Apply economic thinking to the Indian context, helping students understand how concepts like informality, public goods, labor markets, and development policy operate in India's economic landscape.

docs.title: About This Site
docs.text:
This website is an interactive companion to the Ideas in Economics course at FLAME University. Built with MkDocs Material, it provides:

  • Six learning modules, each anchored on a film and a Nobel laureate, with concept explanations, film analysis guides, and self-assessment quizzes.
  • Indian Context essays connecting economic ideas to India's economy and policy.
  • 30+ interactive simulations drawn from Dan McCreary's open-source Introduction to Economics textbook, allowing students to experiment with economic models directly in the browser.
  • Economist Stories --- biographical narratives of influential economists from diverse traditions and backgrounds.
  • A searchable glossary of 120+ economic terms with definitions and examples.

The site is designed to be used alongside classroom instruction and can also serve as a standalone self-study resource. Use the search bar, navigation tabs, and sidebar to move between sections. Dark mode is available via the toggle in the header.

docs.title: Acknowledgements
docs.text: This course and its companion website draw on the work of many educators, researchers, and institutions. The following contributions are gratefully acknowledged.

docs.title: Dan McCreary's Introduction to Economics
docs.text: The interactive simulations (MicroSims) and Economist Stories used throughout this site are drawn from Dan McCreary's open-source Introduction to Economics interactive textbook, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. These browser-based tools --- covering everything from supply and demand to the tragedy of the commons --- allow students to experiment with economic models in real time. The biographical narratives of economists, from Adam Smith to Esther Duflo, provide accessible entry points into the lives and ideas behind the discipline.

docs.title: Textbook Authors
docs.text:
The course syllabus draws on the pedagogical approaches and conceptual frameworks of the following authors, whose works are listed in the References section:

  • Samuel R. Staley --- for the film-and-economics framework that informed the course's structure (Contemporary Film and Economics: Lights! Camera! Econ!).
  • Richard N. Langlois --- for Economics Through Film (ECON 1101, University of Connecticut), a pioneering film-based economics course pairing 12 films with core concepts from institutions to externalities. A key pedagogical model for this course's film-first approach.
  • David Simpson --- for biographical sketches of great economists (Striding with Economic Giants).
  • Larissa Wolfe and Stephen Buckles --- for visual approaches to economic concepts (Easy Economics: A Visual Guide).
  • Ha-Joon Chang --- for a pluralist, accessible introduction to economic schools of thought (Economics: The User's Guide).
  • Irene van Staveren --- for a post-crisis, heterodox perspective on economic reasoning (Economics After The Crisis).
  • Robert H. Frank --- for the art of applying economic thinking to everyday puzzles (The Economic Naturalist).
  • The Nobel Prize Committee --- for the prize lectures, biographies, and popular science summaries available at nobelprize.org.

docs.title: FLAME University
docs.text: This course is offered as part of the undergraduate curriculum at FLAME University, Pune. The university's commitment to a liberal education framework --- emphasizing interdisciplinary thinking, critical inquiry, and real-world application --- is the foundation on which a film-based economics course like this one can exist.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
This glossary defines the key terms used across all six modules. Each entry includes a plain-language definition and a brief example. Terms are listed alphabetically. The Module tag tells you where the concept first appears.

Use ++ctrl+f++ (or ++cmd+f++ on Mac) to search for a specific term.

docs.title: Absolute Poverty
docs.text: A condition where a person's income or consumption falls below a minimum threshold needed to meet basic needs — food, shelter, clothing. Contrasted with relative poverty (being poor compared to others in your society). Example: The World Bank's international poverty line of $2.15/day (2017 PPP) is an absolute poverty measure. India's Tendulkar line serves a similar function domestically. Module 4

docs.title: Adverse Selection
docs.text: A situation where one party in a transaction has more information than the other, leading to a market where low-quality goods or high-risk individuals dominate. Example: If health insurance is voluntary, people who know they are sick are more likely to buy it, driving up premiums for everyone. Module 2

docs.title: Anchoring Bias
docs.text: The tendency to rely too heavily on the first piece of information encountered when making decisions. Example: A shop marks a shirt as "~~₹2,000~~ Now ₹999!" — the ₹2,000 anchor makes ₹999 feel like a bargain, even if the shirt was never worth ₹2,000. Module 1

docs.title: Asymmetric Information
docs.text: A situation where one party in a transaction knows more than the other. Example: A used car seller knows the car's history; the buyer does not. This information gap can lead to adverse selection and moral hazard. Module 2

docs.title: Backward Induction
docs.text: A method of solving sequential games by starting at the final move and reasoning backwards to determine the optimal strategy at each stage. Example: In chess, you think several moves ahead by considering what your opponent will do at each future step. Module 2

docs.title: Behavioral Economics
docs.text: A field that combines insights from psychology and economics to study how people actually make decisions — often deviating from the "rational" predictions of standard economic theory. Example: People spend more using credit cards than cash because the pain of paying feels less immediate. Module 1

docs.title: Bounded Rationality
docs.text: The idea that people's decision-making is limited by the information available, their cognitive abilities, and the time they have to decide. Proposed by Herbert Simon. Example: Rather than comparing every mobile phone on the market, you buy the first one that meets your basic requirements. Module 1

docs.title: Budget Constraint
docs.text: The set of all combinations of goods and services a consumer can afford given their income and prices. Example: With ₹500 per week for food, you can buy 10 meals at ₹50 each, or 5 meals at ₹100, or any combination that totals ₹500. Module 2

docs.title: Capital Deepening
docs.text: An increase in the amount of capital per worker in an economy. In the Solow model, capital deepening raises output per worker but faces diminishing returns. Example: Replacing hand looms with power looms in a textile factory — each worker now has more capital to work with, increasing their productivity. Module 5

docs.title: Carbon Tax
docs.text: A tax levied on the carbon content of fossil fuels, designed to internalize the external cost of greenhouse gas emissions. A form of Pigouvian tax. Example: A carbon tax of $50 per ton of CO2 makes coal-fired electricity more expensive relative to solar, nudging the energy mix toward cleaner sources. Module 6 A market-based system for controlling pollution. The government sets a cap on total emissions and issues tradable permits. Firms that reduce pollution cheaply can sell their permits to firms that find it more expensive. Example: The EU Emissions Trading System covers power plants and factories across Europe. Module 6

docs.title: Capability Approach
docs.text: Amartya Sen's framework that measures well-being not by income alone but by what people are able to do and become — their "capabilities." Example: Two people may earn the same salary, but one lives in a village without schools or hospitals, limiting what they can achieve with that income. Module 4

docs.title: Child Labor
docs.text: The employment of children in work that deprives them of childhood, education, and well-being. Often driven by poverty and lack of alternatives. Example: India's Census 2011 recorded 10.1 million child laborers aged 5-14. The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016 prohibits employment of children below 14 in all occupations. Module 4

docs.title: Common Pool Resource
docs.text: A resource that is rivalrous (one person's use reduces availability for others) but non-excludable (difficult to prevent access). Prone to overuse. Example: Groundwater — each farmer's borewell reduces the water table for all farmers, but no one can be easily excluded from drilling. India has 1,600+ over-exploited groundwater blocks. Module 6

docs.title: Commons Governance
docs.text: Systems of rules, norms, and institutions through which communities manage shared resources. Elinor Ostrom demonstrated that communities can govern commons sustainably without privatization or centralized control. Example: Van Panchayats in Uttarakhand manage ~5,400 sq km of community forests through locally designed rules about harvesting, monitoring, and sanctioning. Module 6 When individuals work together to achieve a common goal that benefits the group. Often difficult because of the free rider problem. Example: Villagers in Uttarakhand's Van Panchayats collectively manage forests, preventing overuse. Module 6

docs.title: Comparative Advantage
docs.text: The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer. A country or person should specialize in what they do relatively best, even if they are not the absolute best at it. Example: India exports IT services not because Indian programmers are the cheapest, but because India's opportunity cost of producing software is lower than its opportunity cost of producing, say, aircraft. Module 3

docs.title: Competition
docs.text: A market structure where many firms sell similar products, and no single firm can control the price. Competition drives innovation and lowers prices. Example: The Indian telecom market after Jio's entry — intense competition drove data prices to among the lowest in the world. Module 2

docs.title: Complementary Goods
docs.text: Goods that are consumed together, so a rise in the price of one reduces demand for the other. Example: Petrol and cars — when petrol prices rise sharply, demand for fuel-inefficient cars falls. Module 3

docs.title: Consumer Surplus
docs.text: The difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay. Example: You would pay ₹200 for a cup of coffee but it costs ₹100 — your consumer surplus is ₹100. Module 3

docs.title: Cooperation
docs.text: When players in a strategic interaction choose to work together rather than compete, often achieving better outcomes for all. Example: OPEC countries cooperate to limit oil production, keeping prices high — though each member is tempted to cheat. Module 2

docs.title: Creative Destruction
docs.text: Joseph Schumpeter's term for the process by which new innovations destroy old industries while creating new ones. Example: Smartphones destroyed the market for separate cameras, music players, and GPS devices — but created entirely new industries like app development. Module 5

docs.title: Credence Good
docs.text: A good or service whose quality the consumer cannot fully evaluate even after consumption. Example: You cannot independently verify whether your mechanic's repair was necessary or whether a doctor's prescription was optimal. Module 2

docs.title: Deadweight Loss
docs.text: The loss of economic efficiency when the equilibrium outcome is not achieved — typically caused by taxes, subsidies, price controls, or monopoly. Example: A price ceiling on rent set below the market rate creates a shortage of apartments, and some willing renters and willing landlords cannot transact. Module 3

docs.title: Demand
docs.text: The quantity of a good or service that consumers are willing and able to purchase at various prices, holding other factors constant. Example: At ₹50 per plate, 100 students buy biryani from the canteen; at ₹80, only 60 buy it. Module 3

docs.title: Diminishing Returns
docs.text: The general principle that increasing one input while holding others constant eventually yields progressively smaller increases in output. Applies broadly to production, investment, and growth. Example: In the Solow growth model, continued capital investment in a country yields smaller and smaller GDP gains — which is why technology, not just investment, drives long-run growth. Module 5

docs.title: Diminishing Marginal Returns
docs.text: The principle that adding more of one input (while holding others constant) eventually produces smaller and smaller increases in output. Example: Adding a second waiter to a small restaurant helps a lot; adding a tenth waiter to the same restaurant adds very little. Module 3

docs.title: Dominant Strategy
docs.text: A strategy that gives the best outcome for a player regardless of what the other player does. Example: In the Prisoner's Dilemma, confessing is a dominant strategy — it gives a better outcome whether the other prisoner confesses or stays silent. Module 2

docs.title: Economic Growth
docs.text: A sustained increase in the total output (GDP) of an economy over time. Can be driven by more inputs (labor, capital) or better technology (TFP growth). Example: India's GDP grew at an average of ~7% per year from 2014-2024, driven by services expansion, demographic dividend, and infrastructure investment. Module 5

docs.title: Economic Mobility
docs.text: The ability of individuals or families to move up (or down) the income or social ladder over time. Example: A rickshaw driver's daughter becomes a software engineer — this represents upward intergenerational mobility. India's economic mobility is constrained by caste, gender, and geography. Module 4

docs.title: Economic Model
docs.text: A simplified representation of an economic process or relationship, used to make predictions and analyze policy. Models deliberately leave out details to focus on key mechanisms. Example: The supply-and-demand model assumes many buyers and sellers, but ignores the fact that real markets have advertising, brand loyalty, and information gaps. Module 1

docs.title: Economies of Scale
docs.text: Cost advantages that firms gain as production increases — the cost per unit falls as output rises. Example: Tata Motors can produce cars at a lower per-unit cost than a small workshop because it spreads fixed costs (factory, machinery) over millions of vehicles. Module 5

docs.title: Education Returns
docs.text: The economic gains from investing in education — measured as the percentage increase in earnings for each additional year of schooling. Also called "returns to education." Example: In India, completing secondary school increases average earnings by approximately 15-20% compared to primary school only, though returns vary by gender, caste, and region. Module 4

docs.title: Efficiency
docs.text: An allocation of resources where no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off (Pareto efficiency). Example: An economy operating on its Production Possibilities Frontier is productively efficient — it cannot produce more of one good without producing less of another. Module 1

docs.title: Elasticity
docs.text: A measure of how responsive quantity demanded or supplied is to a change in price or income. Example: Salt has low price elasticity (people buy roughly the same amount even if the price doubles); airline tickets have high elasticity (a small price drop can greatly increase bookings). Module 3

docs.title: Endowment Effect
docs.text: The tendency for people to value something more highly once they own it. Example: In Thaler's mug experiment, students who received a mug demanded ~$7 to sell it, while those who did not own one were willing to pay only ~$3. Module 1

docs.title: Equilibrium
docs.text: A state where no participant has an incentive to change their behavior, given what others are doing. In a market, it is the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Example: If the market price of wheat is ₹25/kg, and at that price farmers want to sell exactly as much as consumers want to buy, the market is in equilibrium. Module 3

docs.title: Externality
docs.text: A cost or benefit of a transaction that affects a third party who did not choose to be involved. Example: A factory pollutes a river (negative externality), harming downstream farmers who had no say in the factory's production decisions. Module 6

docs.title: Financial Crisis
docs.text: A sudden, widespread disruption of financial markets, typically involving bank failures, credit freezes, and sharp declines in asset prices. Example: The 2008 global financial crisis began with the collapse of the US housing bubble and spread through interconnected financial institutions worldwide. Module 1

docs.title: Fiscal Policy
docs.text: Government decisions about spending and taxation to influence the economy. Example: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Indian government announced the Atmanirbhar Bharat package to boost economic activity through increased spending. Module 3

docs.title: Free Rider Problem
docs.text: When individuals benefit from a resource or service without paying for it, because they cannot be excluded. Example: If a neighborhood hires a private security guard, residents who do not contribute still benefit from the reduced crime. Module 6

docs.title: Framing Effect
docs.text: The tendency for people to react differently to the same information depending on how it is presented. Example: Patients are more likely to agree to surgery if told "90% survive" than if told "10% die" — the information is identical, but the frame changes the decision. Module 1

docs.title: Free Rider
docs.text: A person who benefits from a shared resource or collective effort without contributing their fair share. The free rider problem makes it difficult for private markets to provide public goods. Example: A resident who enjoys the neighborhood park maintained by community donations but never donates themselves. Module 6

docs.title: GDP Per Capita
docs.text: A country's total GDP divided by its population. A rough measure of average economic well-being, though it hides inequality. Example: India's GDP per capita in 2024 was approximately $2,700 — far below China ($13,000) or the US ($80,000), reflecting both India's large population and lower productivity. Module 5

docs.title: Gender Gap
docs.text: The systematic difference between men and women in economic outcomes — wages, labor force participation, education, or political representation. Example: India's female labor force participation rate is approximately 37% (PLFS 2024), compared to over 70% for men — one of the widest gender gaps in the world. Module 4

docs.title: Globalization
docs.text: The increasing integration of national economies through trade, investment, migration, and information flows. Example: An iPhone designed in California, assembled in China from components made in Japan, South Korea, and India, sold worldwide — this supply chain is globalization in action. India's IT exports ($200+ billion) are both a product and driver of globalization. Module 3 The study of strategic interactions where the outcome for each participant depends on the decisions of others. Example: Two competing telecom companies deciding whether to lower prices — each company's best move depends on what the other does. Module 2

docs.title: GDP (Gross Domestic Product)
docs.text: The total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period. Example: India's GDP in 2024-25 was approximately $3.9 trillion, making it the world's fifth-largest economy. Module 5

docs.title: Gini Coefficient
docs.text: A measure of income inequality ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality). Example: India's Gini coefficient is approximately 0.35, indicating moderate inequality — higher than many European countries but lower than Brazil or South Africa. Module 4

docs.title: Herd Behavior
docs.text: When individuals follow the actions of a larger group, often ignoring their own information or analysis. Example: Investors piling into the stock market because "everyone else is making money" — a pattern that fuels market bubbles. Module 1

docs.title: Heuristics
docs.text: Mental shortcuts that people use to make decisions quickly. While often useful, heuristics can lead to systematic biases. Example: The "availability heuristic" — people overestimate the risk of plane crashes (dramatic, memorable events) and underestimate the risk of car accidents (common, unremarkable). Module 2

docs.title: Human Capital
docs.text: The skills, knowledge, and experience possessed by workers that make them productive. Investment in human capital (education, training, health) increases earning potential. Example: A software engineer who learns a new programming language increases their human capital and, typically, their salary. Module 5

docs.title: Human Development Index (HDI)
docs.text: A composite measure of well-being combining life expectancy, education, and income per capita. Created by the UNDP, based on Amartya Sen's capability approach. Example: Kerala ranks among India's highest HDI states despite modest per-capita income, because of strong performance in health and education. Module 4

docs.title: Incentive
docs.text: A reward or penalty that motivates behavior. Economics assumes that people respond to incentives. Example: A congestion charge in central London incentivizes drivers to use public transport, reducing traffic. In India, MGNREGA's wage guarantee incentivizes rural workers to participate in public works. Module 1

docs.title: Inequality
docs.text: The uneven distribution of income, wealth, or opportunities across a population. Measured by the Gini coefficient, Palma ratio, or income share of the top/bottom groups. Example: India's top 10% hold approximately 57% of national income (World Inequality Lab), while the bottom 50% hold about 13%. Module 4

docs.title: Informal Economy
docs.text: Economic activity that operates outside formal regulations, taxation, and social protection systems. Includes self-employment, casual labor, and small unregistered enterprises. Example: Street vendors, domestic workers, and construction day-laborers — approximately 90% of India's workforce is informal, contributing roughly 50% of GDP. Module 4

docs.title: Income Elasticity of Demand
docs.text: A measure of how demand for a good changes when consumer income changes. Example: As Indian household incomes rise, demand for two-wheelers (normal goods) increases, while demand for kerosene (inferior good) decreases. Module 3

docs.title: Inferior Good
docs.text: A good for which demand decreases as consumer income rises. Example: Coarse grain — as incomes rise in rural India, families switch to rice or wheat. Module 3

docs.title: Information Asymmetry
docs.text: See Asymmetric Information. Module 2

docs.title: Innovation
docs.text: The introduction of new products, processes, or ideas that create value. Can be radical (entirely new) or incremental (improving existing products). Example: UPI was a radical innovation in digital payments; each successive version with new features represents incremental innovation. Module 5

docs.title: Institutions
docs.text: The formal rules (laws, regulations) and informal norms (customs, trust) that structure economic and social interactions. Example: Property rights, contract enforcement, and anti-corruption laws are institutions that determine whether markets function well. India's weak land title system is an institutional barrier to investment. Module 2

docs.title: Labor Market
docs.text: The market where workers supply their labor and firms demand it. Wages are the "price" in this market. Example: India's labor market includes ~500 million workers, of whom approximately 90% are in the informal sector without written contracts or social security. Module 3

docs.title: Law of Demand
docs.text: All else equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, and vice versa. Example: When Zomato offers a 50% discount, orders surge; when the discount is removed, orders fall. Module 3

docs.title: Law of Supply
docs.text: All else equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises, and vice versa. Example: When onion prices spike, more farmers rush to bring their stored onions to market. Module 3

docs.title: Loss Aversion
docs.text: The tendency for people to feel the pain of a loss more intensely than the pleasure of an equivalent gain — roughly twice as much. Example: Losing ₹100 feels worse than finding ₹100 feels good. This explains why investors hold losing stocks too long — selling would "realize" the loss. Module 1

docs.title: Marginal Benefit
docs.text: The additional benefit gained from consuming one more unit of a good or service. Example: The first glass of water on a hot day is extremely valuable; the fifth glass is much less so. Module 1

docs.title: Marginal Cost
docs.text: The additional cost of producing one more unit of a good or service. Example: If a factory produces 100 shirts at ₹50,000 total and 101 shirts at ₹50,400 total, the marginal cost of the 101st shirt is ₹400. Module 1

docs.title: Marginal Thinking
docs.text: Making decisions by comparing the additional benefit of an action to its additional cost — one unit at a time. Example: "Should I study one more hour?" depends on whether the extra marks gained (marginal benefit) are worth the sleep lost (marginal cost). Module 1

docs.title: Market Bubble
docs.text: A situation where the price of an asset rises far above its fundamental value, driven by speculation and herd behavior, and eventually collapses. Example: The US housing bubble of 2003-2007, where house prices were driven up by speculative buying and easy credit, culminating in the 2008 financial crisis. Module 1

docs.title: Market Equilibrium
docs.text: See Equilibrium. Module 3

docs.title: Market Failure
docs.text: A situation where the free market does not allocate resources efficiently, justifying potential government intervention. Causes include externalities, public goods, monopoly, and information asymmetry. Example: Air pollution is a market failure because the polluter does not bear the full cost of the harm caused. Module 6

docs.title: Mental Accounting
docs.text: The tendency to treat money differently depending on where it comes from or how it is categorized, violating the economic principle that money is fungible. Example: Spending a tax refund on a luxury item ("bonus money") while simultaneously carrying credit card debt at 18% interest. Module 1

docs.title: Microfinance
docs.text: Small loans and financial services provided to low-income individuals who lack access to traditional banking. Example: Self-Help Groups (SHGs) in India pool savings and provide small loans to members, reaching over 100 million women. Module 4

docs.title: Monopoly
docs.text: A market structure with a single seller and no close substitutes. A monopolist can set prices above competitive levels. Example: Indian Railways is effectively a monopoly in long-distance rail transport — there is no competing rail service on the same routes. Module 3

docs.title: Moral Hazard
docs.text: When someone takes greater risks because they do not bear the full consequences of their actions. Example: Mortgage brokers in The Big Short issued risky loans because they earned commissions regardless of whether borrowers repaid — the risk was passed to investors. In India, the IL&FS crisis involved similar risk-shifting through the NBFC sector. Module 1

docs.title: Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)
docs.text: A measure of poverty that considers multiple deprivations — health, education, and living standards — not just income. Example: According to NITI Aayog's 2023 report, India's MPI headcount ratio declined from 24.85% in 2015-16 to 14.96% in 2019-21. Module 4

docs.title: Nash Equilibrium
docs.text: A set of strategies in a game where no player can improve their outcome by changing their strategy alone, given what the other players are doing. Named after John Nash. Example: In a duopoly where both firms charge moderate prices, neither firm benefits from unilaterally raising its price (losing customers) or lowering it (starting a price war). Module 2

docs.title: Natural Monopoly
docs.text: An industry where a single firm can supply the entire market at lower cost than two or more firms, typically due to high fixed costs. Example: Electricity distribution — it makes no sense to have two competing sets of power lines running to every home. Module 3

docs.title: Negative Externality
docs.text: A cost imposed on third parties who are not part of a transaction. Example: A coal power plant emits pollution that causes respiratory illness in nearby communities — the health costs are borne by residents, not the power company. Module 6

docs.title: Network Effects
docs.text: When the value of a product or service increases as more people use it. Example: WhatsApp is valuable because almost everyone in India uses it — a messaging app used by only 10 people has little value. Module 5

docs.title: Normal Good
docs.text: A good for which demand increases as consumer income rises. Example: Restaurant meals — as families earn more, they eat out more frequently. Module 3

docs.title: Normative Economics
docs.text: See Positive Economics. Module 1

docs.title: Nudge
docs.text: A small change in how choices are presented ("choice architecture") that steers people toward better decisions without restricting their freedom to choose otherwise. Coined by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein. Example: Making organ donation the default option (opt-out rather than opt-in) dramatically increases donation rates. India's Swachh Bharat Mission used social norms messaging as a nudge. Module 1

docs.title: Oligopoly
docs.text: A market dominated by a small number of large firms, where each firm's actions affect the others. Example: India's telecom market — dominated by Jio, Airtel, and Vodafone Idea — is an oligopoly where pricing and investment decisions are highly strategic. Module 3

docs.title: Opportunity Cost
docs.text: The value of the best alternative that you give up when you make a choice. The true cost of any decision. Example: If you spend Saturday studying instead of working a shift that pays ₹500, the opportunity cost of studying is ₹500 (assuming the job was your next-best option). Module 1

docs.title: Pareto Efficiency
docs.text: See Efficiency. Module 1

docs.title: Perfect Competition
docs.text: A theoretical market structure with many small firms selling identical products, free entry and exit, and perfect information. No single firm can influence the market price. Example: Agricultural commodity markets approximate perfect competition — thousands of wheat farmers sell a homogeneous product and individually have no power over the price. Module 3 See Efficiency. Module 1

docs.title: Pigouvian Tax
docs.text: A tax on activities that generate negative externalities, designed to make the private cost equal the social cost. Named after economist Arthur Pigou. Example: A carbon tax that charges firms for each ton of CO2 emitted, internalizing the environmental cost. Module 6

docs.title: Platform Economy
docs.text: Economic activity organized through digital platforms that connect buyers and sellers, workers and firms, or users and content. Example: Swiggy, Uber, and Amazon are platforms — they do not produce the goods or services themselves but facilitate transactions between others. Module 5

docs.title: Positive Externality
docs.text: A benefit that accrues to third parties who are not involved in a transaction. Example: When you get vaccinated, you protect not only yourself but also people around you (herd immunity). Education also generates positive externalities — educated workers raise productivity for their colleagues and contribute to civic life. Module 6

docs.title: Price Mechanism
docs.text: The process by which prices coordinate the decisions of buyers and sellers in a market. Rising prices signal scarcity and encourage conservation; falling prices signal abundance and encourage consumption. Example: When onion prices spike due to a poor harvest, consumers reduce purchases and other farmers rush supply to market — the price mechanism coordinates these responses without any central planner. Module 3

docs.title: Private Good
docs.text: A good that is both excludable (non-payers can be prevented from consuming it) and rivalrous (one person's consumption reduces what is available for others). Most market goods are private goods. Example: A sandwich — if you eat it, no one else can, and the seller can refuse to give it to you unless you pay. Module 6 Economic statements about facts — claims that can be tested with evidence ("what is"). Contrasted with normative economics, which involves value judgments about "what ought to be." Example: "Raising the minimum wage to ₹300/day will reduce employment in small firms by 5%" is a positive statement (testable). "The minimum wage should be ₹300/day" is a normative statement (a value judgment). Module 1

docs.title: Poverty Line
docs.text: A threshold income or consumption level below which a person is classified as poor. Example: India's official poverty line (Tendulkar methodology) was set at ₹816/month in rural areas and ₹1,000/month in urban areas (2011-12 prices). Debate continues about whether these thresholds are adequate. Module 4

docs.title: Price Ceiling
docs.text: A legal maximum price that can be charged for a good or service. If set below the market equilibrium, it creates a shortage. Example: Rent control in Mumbai — by capping rents below market rates, the policy discourages new construction and creates a shortage of affordable housing. Module 3

docs.title: Price Floor
docs.text: A legal minimum price. If set above the market equilibrium, it creates a surplus. Example: India's Minimum Support Price (MSP) for wheat guarantees farmers a price above the market rate, encouraging production but sometimes creating government stockpile surpluses. Module 3

docs.title: Prisoner's Dilemma
docs.text: A game theory scenario where two rational individuals might not cooperate even when cooperation would benefit both, because each has an incentive to defect. Example: Two competing firms would both profit more by keeping prices high, but each is tempted to undercut the other — so both end up with low prices and low profits. Module 2

docs.title: Producer Surplus
docs.text: The difference between the price a producer receives and the minimum price they would accept. Example: A farmer willing to sell wheat at ₹20/kg but receiving the MSP of ₹25/kg earns a producer surplus of ₹5/kg. Module 3

docs.title: Production Possibilities Frontier
docs.text: A curve showing the maximum possible combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its available resources and technology. Points on the curve are efficient; points inside are inefficient; points outside are unattainable. Example: India's Union Budget illustrates the PPF — more spending on infrastructure means less available for subsidies, unless the economy grows. Module 1

docs.title: Productivity
docs.text: The amount of output produced per unit of input (labor, capital, or both). Higher productivity means more output from the same resources. Example: Mechanized farming produces more grain per worker-hour than manual farming. India's relatively low labor productivity is a major policy concern. Module 5

docs.title: Property Rights
docs.text: Legal rules that define who owns a resource and what they can do with it. Well-defined property rights are essential for markets to function. Example: Unclear land titles in rural India discourage investment because farmers cannot use their land as collateral for loans. Module 2

docs.title: Public Good
docs.text: A good that is non-excludable (you cannot prevent people from using it) and non-rivalrous (one person's use does not reduce availability for others). Example: National defense, street lighting, and clean air are public goods. Because people can free-ride, private markets typically under-provide them. Module 6

docs.title: Regulation
docs.text: Government rules that constrain or direct economic behavior. Can address market failures (pollution standards, safety requirements) but can also create inefficiencies (excessive compliance costs, rent-seeking). Example: India's Bureau of Energy Efficiency star ratings for appliances — a regulation that uses information provision to steer consumer choices toward energy-efficient products. Module 6

docs.title: Relative Poverty
docs.text: Being poor relative to the standards of one's own society — typically defined as having income below a certain percentage (e.g., 60%) of the median. Contrasted with absolute poverty. Example: A family in Mumbai earning ₹15,000/month is above the absolute poverty line but may be in relative poverty given the high cost of urban living. Module 4

docs.title: Research and Development
docs.text: Systematic investment in creating new knowledge (research) and applying it to create new products or processes (development). A key driver of innovation and long-run growth. Example: India's R&D spending is approximately 0.7% of GDP — significantly below China (2.4%) and the US (3.5%), which partly explains the innovation gap. Module 5 An experimental method where participants are randomly assigned to a treatment group or a control group to measure the causal effect of an intervention. Example: Esther Duflo and Abhijit Banerjee used RCTs to test whether providing free bed nets (rather than selling them cheaply) increased malaria prevention in Africa. Module 4

docs.title: Rational Choice
docs.text: The assumption that people have clear preferences, weigh costs and benefits, and choose the option that maximizes their well-being. A foundational assumption of standard economics. Example: A rational consumer compares prices, quality, and alternatives before purchasing a phone. In practice, people often rely on brand loyalty, social proof, or impulse. Module 1

docs.title: Rent-Seeking
docs.text: Using resources to influence policy or regulations to gain economic advantage without creating new value. Example: A firm lobbying the government for a monopoly license rather than competing on quality and price. The "License Raj" era in India (pre-1991) was characterized by extensive rent-seeking. Module 3

docs.title: Shortage
docs.text: A situation where the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied at the current price. Often caused by price ceilings or supply disruptions. Example: When the government caps the price of essential medicines below the market rate, pharmacies may run out of stock because suppliers find it unprofitable to sell at that price. Module 3

docs.title: Social Safety Net
docs.text: Government programs that provide a minimum level of support to vulnerable populations — through cash transfers, food subsidies, employment guarantees, or insurance. Example: India's social safety net includes MGNREGA (employment guarantee), PDS (food rations), PM-KISAN (cash transfers to farmers), and Ayushman Bharat (health insurance for 500 million poor). Module 4

docs.title: Solow Model
docs.text: See Solow Growth Model. Module 5 The fundamental economic problem: human wants are unlimited, but resources (time, money, land, labor, raw materials) are finite. Scarcity forces choices. Example: Even a billionaire faces scarcity of time. India faces scarcity of clean water despite being a large economy. Module 1

docs.title: Social Cost
docs.text: The total cost of an activity to society, including both private costs borne by the producer and external costs borne by third parties. Example: The social cost of driving includes the driver's fuel and time (private costs) plus pollution, congestion, and accident risk imposed on others (external costs). Module 6

docs.title: Solow Growth Model
docs.text: Robert Solow's framework showing that long-run economic growth depends primarily on technological progress, not just accumulating more capital or labor. Example: The model explains why simply building more factories (capital accumulation) eventually faces diminishing returns — sustained growth requires innovation. Module 5

docs.title: Strategic Interaction
docs.text: A situation where the outcome of your decision depends on the decisions made by others. The central subject of game theory. Example: A firm deciding whether to launch a new product must consider how competitors will respond — will they match the price, launch their own version, or ignore it? Module 2

docs.title: Subsidy
docs.text: A payment from the government to producers or consumers intended to encourage production or consumption of a good. Example: India's fertilizer subsidy makes agricultural inputs cheaper for farmers, but costs the government over ₹1.5 lakh crore annually and can distort market signals. Module 3

docs.title: Substitute Goods
docs.text: Goods that can replace each other, so a rise in the price of one increases demand for the other. Example: Tea and coffee — when coffee prices rise, some consumers switch to tea. Module 3

docs.title: Sunk Cost
docs.text: A cost that has already been incurred and cannot be recovered, regardless of future decisions. Rational decision-makers should ignore sunk costs. Example: You paid ₹2,000 for a non-refundable train ticket but get a better offer. The ₹2,000 is sunk — your decision should depend only on which option you prefer now, not on the money already spent. Module 1

docs.title: Surplus
docs.text: A situation where the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded at the current price. Often caused by price floors. Example: When the government sets the Minimum Support Price for wheat above the market equilibrium, farmers produce more than consumers want to buy at that price, creating a surplus that the government must procure and store. Module 3

docs.title: Sustainability
docs.text: Meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Requires balancing economic growth with environmental preservation and social equity. Example: India's International Solar Alliance promotes sustainable energy transition — solar capacity grew from 2.6 GW in 2014 to 82+ GW in 2024, reducing dependence on coal without sacrificing growth. Module 6

docs.title: Supply
docs.text: The quantity of a good or service that producers are willing and able to sell at various prices, holding other factors constant. Example: At ₹80/kg, onion farmers bring 10,000 tonnes to market; at ₹40/kg, only 5,000 tonnes. Module 3

docs.title: Systemic Risk
docs.text: The risk that the failure of one institution or market triggers a cascade of failures across the entire financial system. Example: The collapse of Lehman Brothers in 2008 triggered a global credit freeze because Lehman was deeply interconnected with other financial institutions. India's IL&FS default in 2018 created similar contagion fears in the NBFC sector. Module 1

docs.title: Technological Change
docs.text: Improvements in the methods or tools used to produce goods and services. Can be embodied (in new machines) or disembodied (new organizational methods). The primary driver of long-run economic growth in the Solow model. Example: The shift from manual record-keeping to computerized databases — the same number of clerks can process far more transactions. Module 5

docs.title: Technology Residual
docs.text: See Total Factor Productivity. Module 5

docs.title: Total Factor Productivity
docs.text: The portion of output growth that cannot be explained by increases in labor or capital inputs — often attributed to technological progress, efficiency improvements, or institutional quality. Also called the "Solow residual." Example: If India's GDP grows by 7% but labor and capital together explain only 4%, the remaining 3% is TFP growth. Module 5

docs.title: Trade-off
docs.text: The sacrifice of one thing in order to get something else. Every choice involves a trade-off because resources are scarce. Example: Studying an extra hour for your exam means one less hour of sleep — you trade rest for better preparation. Module 1

docs.title: Tragedy of the Commons
docs.text: The depletion of a shared resource when individuals act in their own self-interest without coordination. Example: Overfishing in the open ocean — each fishing boat takes as much as it can, and the collective result is collapse of fish stocks. India's groundwater crisis follows the same logic. Module 6

docs.title: Unemployment
docs.text: The state of being without work while actively seeking employment. Can be frictional (between jobs), structural (skills mismatch), or cyclical (due to economic downturns). Example: India's PLFS 2024 reports an unemployment rate of approximately 3.2% — but this masks significant underemployment and disguised unemployment in the informal sector. Module 3

docs.title: Utility
docs.text: A measure of satisfaction or happiness that a consumer derives from consuming a good or service. Example: The first slice of pizza gives high utility; by the fourth slice, utility is much lower — illustrating diminishing marginal utility. Module 2

docs.title: Value Added
docs.text: The increase in value that a firm contributes to a product at each stage of production. Example: A cotton farmer sells raw cotton for ₹50/kg. A spinning mill converts it to yarn worth ₹120/kg. The mill's value added is ₹70/kg. Module 5

docs.title: Wage Determination
docs.text: The process by which wages are set in a labor market — through supply and demand, collective bargaining, minimum wage laws, or employer market power. Example: In India's IT sector, wages are largely determined by market supply and demand (competitive labor market). In the organized manufacturing sector, union bargaining plays a larger role. MGNREGA sets a floor through its guaranteed wage. Module 3 The price of labor — the payment workers receive for their services. Determined by supply and demand in the labor market, influenced by skills, experience, bargaining power, and institutional factors like minimum wage laws. Example: MGNREGA guarantees a minimum wage (₹267-374/day depending on state) for unskilled manual labor in rural areas. Module 3

docs.title: Willingness to Pay
docs.text:
The maximum amount a consumer would pay for a good or service. Example: If you would pay up to ₹150 for a movie ticket but the price is ₹100, your willingness to pay is ₹150 and your consumer surplus is ₹50. Module 3

This glossary covers approximately 90 terms used across all six modules. Terms are cross-referenced where relevant. For deeper exploration, see the Module pages and Resources.

docs.title: How to Use This Site
docs.text: This site is your interactive companion for the Ideas in Economics course. It is designed to be used alongside classroom sessions, but it also works as a standalone self-study resource. Here is how to get the most out of it.

docs.title: How the Site Is Organized
docs.text:
The site has the following main sections, accessible from the navigation tabs at the top of every page:

Section What You Will Find Modules Six learning modules, each built around a film and a Nobel laureate. Every module contains concept explanations, a film analysis guide, a Nobel Focus profile, a self-assessment quiz, and additional resources. Indian Context Five essays connecting course topics to the Indian economy --- informality, Digital India, NREGA, GST, and climate commons. Interactive Sims 30+ browser-based simulations organized by module, covering everything from supply and demand to the tragedy of the commons. Economist Stories Biographical narratives of 15 influential economists, from Adam Smith to Esther Duflo, organized by module relevance. Glossary 120+ economic terms with definitions and examples, searchable and cross-referenced. References Suggested textbooks and additional readings from the Calibre library.

docs.title: Recommended Workflow
docs.text:
For each module, follow this sequence:

  1. Read the module content. Start with the module's main page, which introduces the core economic concepts for that topic.
  2. Watch the film. Each module is anchored on a specific film. Watch it before or alongside reading the module --- the film analysis guide will help you spot the economic ideas embedded in the narrative.
  3. Read the Nobel Focus. Understand how a Nobel laureate's research connects to the module's theme.
  4. Explore the simulations. Open the interactive sims linked to that module. Adjust sliders, change parameters, and observe how economic models respond. These are the best way to build intuition.
  5. Take the quiz. Each module ends with a 10-question self-assessment. Use it to check your understanding before moving on.
  6. Read the Indian Context essay. See how the module's concepts apply to India's economy and policy landscape.

You do not need to complete all steps in a single sitting. The site saves no progress, so bookmark pages you want to return to.

docs.title: Using Search
docs.text:
The search bar (top of every page, or press ++s++ on your keyboard) is one of the most useful features. Type any economic term, film title, economist's name, or concept, and the site will show matching results across all sections with highlighted snippets.

Search suggestions appear as you type, making it easy to jump directly to the right page.

docs.title: Navigating Between Sections
docs.text:
• Top navigation tabs switch between major sections (Modules, Indian Context, Sims, Stories, etc.).
  • The left sidebar shows the pages within the current section. In the Modules section, you can expand each module to see its sub-pages (Content, Film, Nobel, Quiz, Resources).
  • The right sidebar (on wider screens) shows the table of contents for the current page, so you can jump to any heading.
  • The "Back to top" button appears when you scroll down --- click it to return to the top of any long page.
  • Dark mode is available via the brightness toggle icon in the header bar.

docs.title: About the Interactive Simulations
docs.text:
The interactive simulations on this site are drawn from Dan McCreary's Introduction to Economics open textbook, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

When you click a simulation link, it opens on the McCreary site in a new tab. The simulations run entirely in your browser --- no installation or login is required. They work best on a laptop or desktop screen, though most are functional on tablets as well.

Each simulation includes brief instructions. Experiment freely: adjust inputs, observe outputs, and try to predict what will happen before you make a change. That habit of prediction and verification is at the heart of economic reasoning.

docs.title: Suggested Readings and Textbooks
docs.text:
The following texts form the core reading list for the course. They are referenced across modules and provide the conceptual foundations for the film-based discussions.

  1. Staley, S. R. (2018). Contemporary Film and Economics: Lights! Camera! Econ! The foundational text for the course's approach --- using feature films as a lens for economic analysis.

  2. Simpson, D. (2023). Striding with Economic Giants. Business Expert Press. Biographical sketches of the economists whose ideas shaped modern economics, paired with the Nobel Focus sections in each module.

  3. Wolfe, L. & Buckles, S. (2011). Easy Economics: A Visual Guide. An accessible, diagram-rich introduction to core economic concepts --- useful as a quick reference alongside module readings.

  4. Chang, H.-J. (2014). Economics: The User's Guide. A pluralist overview of the major schools of economic thought, written for a general audience. Excellent for understanding why economists disagree.

  5. van Staveren, I. (2015). Economics After The Crisis. A post-crisis introduction that brings institutional, post-Keynesian, and social economics perspectives into dialogue with the mainstream.

  6. Frank, R. H. (2011). The Economic Naturalist. Ebury Publishing. Short, puzzle-based essays that demonstrate how economic reasoning applies to everyday observations --- a model for the kind of thinking the course aims to develop.

  7. nobelprize.org --- nobelprize.org. Prize lectures, biographies, and popular science summaries for all Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences laureates. Used throughout the Nobel Focus sections.

  8. Langlois, R. N. Economics Through Film (ECON 1101). University of Connecticut. Course page. A pioneering film-based economics course pairing 12 films (including The Big Short, Moneyball, and Dr. Strangelove) with concepts from institutions and property rights to game theory and externalities. No textbook --- readings drawn from Smith, Keynes, and contemporary sources. A key inspiration for this course's film-first pedagogy.

docs.title: Additional Resources (Calibre Library)
docs.text:
The following books are available in the course's digital library and provide supplementary reading across all six modules. They are not required, but students seeking deeper engagement with economic ideas will find them valuable.

  1. Yueh, Linda. What Would the Great Economists Do? Profiles of history's most influential economists and what their ideas mean for contemporary challenges.

  2. Wheelan, Charles. Naked Economics: Undressing the Dismal Science. A lively, jargon-free introduction to how economies work, widely used as a gateway text.

  3. Varoufakis, Yanis. Talking to My Daughter About the Economy: A Brief History of Capitalism. A narrative-driven explanation of how market economies emerged and why they produce inequality.

  4. How Economics Should Be Done: Essays on the Art and Craft of Economics. Reflections on methodology and practice in economics.

  5. Komlos, John. Foundations of Real-World Economics: What Every Economics Student Needs to Know. A heterodox textbook that foregrounds real-world applications, behavioral insights, and policy relevance.

  6. Free, Rhona C. (ed.) 21st Century Economics: A Reference Handbook. A comprehensive reference covering major fields and debates in modern economics.

  7. The Nobel Memorial Laureates in Economics: An Introduction to Their Careers and Main Published Works. A reference guide to the laureates discussed in the Nobel Focus sections.

  8. Buchholz, Todd G. New Ideas from Dead Economists: An Introduction to Modern Economic Thought. An engaging intellectual history from Adam Smith to modern macroeconomics --- pairs well with the Economist Stories section.

  9. Sanders, Shane. The Economic Reason. Short essays on the logic of economic thinking, suitable for students encountering the discipline for the first time.

  10. Lewis, Hunter. Economics in Three Lessons & One Hundred Economic Laws. A concise summary of core economic principles organized around three foundational lessons.

  11. Landsburg, Steven E. Can You Outsmart an Economist? 100+ Puzzles to Train Your Brain. Puzzle-based economic reasoning --- an entertaining complement to the problem sets.

  12. Campbell, Rebecca. How to Teach Economics to Your Dog. An accessible, conversational introduction to economics using everyday examples.

  13. Leyden, Dennis Patrick. Thinking Critically in Economics. A guide to developing the analytical and argumentative skills needed for economic reasoning --- useful for the empirical project.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: Economics is a way of understanding the world. This course uses films as a gateway to introduce fundamental economic concepts. Through movie analysis and Nobel Prize-winning research, students explore market behavior, incentives, labor dynamics, development, and policy. The course also serves as a foundation for further study in microeconomics and macroeconomics.

docs.title: Course Objectives
docs.text:
1. Introduce core economic concepts through accessible, real-world narratives drawn from cinema, enabling students to connect abstract ideas to concrete situations.
  2. Develop economic reasoning skills by analyzing trade-offs, incentives, market behavior, and strategic interactions as depicted in feature films.
  3. Expose students to landmark economic research by pairing each module with the work of a Nobel Prize-winning economist, grounding film-based discussions in rigorous scholarship.
  4. Apply economic thinking to the Indian context, helping students understand how concepts like informality, public goods, labor markets, and development policy operate in India's economic landscape.

docs.title: Expected Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
Upon completing this course, students will be able to:

# Learning Outcome REM UND APP ANA EVA CRE 1 Identify and explain foundational economic concepts such as scarcity, opportunity cost, supply and demand, market equilibrium, and externalities. H H M L -- -- 2 Analyze economic behavior and institutional dynamics as portrayed in feature films, connecting narrative elements to formal economic reasoning. -- M H H M -- 3 Evaluate the contributions of Nobel Prize-winning economists and relate their research to real-world economic phenomena and policy debates. -- M M H H L 4 Apply economic frameworks to understand contemporary issues in the Indian economy, including informality, labor markets, poverty, and environmental challenges. -- L H H M M

REM = Remember, UND = Understand, APP = Apply, ANA = Analyze, EVA = Evaluate, CRE = Create. H = High, M = Medium, L = Low, -- = Not applicable.

docs.text:

Total contact hours: 18

docs.title: Assessment Plan
docs.text: Component Weight Description End-Term Empirical Project 40% A group empirical project applying economic concepts from the course to a real-world question, with data analysis and a written report. Mid-Term Examination 30% Written examination covering Modules 1--3, including conceptual questions, short-answer problems, and film-based analysis. Problem Sets 20% Four to five problem sets distributed across the semester, requiring application of economic reasoning to scenarios, data, and film content. Participation 10% Active engagement in classroom discussions, film screenings, and in-class activities.

docs.title: Suggested Pedagogy
docs.text:
This course adopts an interactive, film-based pedagogical approach. Each module begins with a feature film screening (or assigned viewing) that introduces students to the module's economic themes through narrative. Classroom sessions then unpack the economic concepts embedded in the film, using guided discussion, worked examples, and short problem-solving exercises.

Nobel Prize-winning research is woven into each module to connect popular narratives with frontier scholarship. Interactive browser-based simulations allow students to experiment with economic models --- supply and demand, externalities, game theory --- in real time. Indian Context essays and case studies ground the material in the local economic environment, ensuring relevance beyond the textbook.

The assessment design emphasizes progressive engagement: problem sets build analytical skills throughout the semester, the mid-term tests conceptual mastery of the first half, and the end-term empirical project requires students to synthesize the full course into an original, evidence-based analysis.

  4. Chang, H.-J. (2014). Economics: The User's Guide.
  5. van Staveren, I. (2015). Economics After The Crisis.
  6. Frank, R. H. (2011). The Economic Naturalist. Ebury Publishing.

  8. Langlois, R. N. Economics Through Film (ECON 1101). University of Connecticut. A film-based economics course pairing 12 films with core concepts --- a key pedagogical model for this course.

docs.title: Indian Context
docs.text:
Economics is not just theory locked inside textbooks. The same concepts — scarcity, incentives, market failure, public goods — play out differently depending on a country's history, institutions, and politics. India, with 1.4 billion people, a federal democracy, and an economy that spans subsistence farming and cutting-edge software exports, offers some of the richest and most complex illustrations of economic principles anywhere in the world.

These five essays take ideas you encounter in your course modules and ground them in Indian reality. You will see how the informal economy makes scarcity and labor markets visible in ways that formal statistics often miss. You will examine how digital infrastructure like UPI and Aadhaar represent both technological innovation and a massive experiment in choice architecture. You will study MGNREGA as a case study in incentive design, GST as an attempt to unify fragmented markets, and community forestry as an example of governing the commons without privatization or central control.

Each essay is self-contained — you can read them in any order. But together, they tell a larger story: economic ideas are not abstract principles that exist apart from society. They are tools that real people use, adapt, and sometimes struggle with, in the messy business of building a better economy.
