docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Externalities are costs or benefits that fall on people not party to a transaction — they cause markets to produce the wrong quantity.
  2. Negative externalities (pollution, congestion) lead to overproduction; positive externalities (education, vaccination) lead to underproduction.
  3. Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable — the free rider problem makes private provision inadequate.
  4. Common pool resources are rival but non-excludable — they are vulnerable to the Tragedy of the Commons.
  5. Pigouvian taxes correct externalities by making polluters pay the social cost — using the price mechanism rather than fighting it.
  6. Cap-and-trade sets an overall pollution limit and lets the market find the cheapest way to achieve it.
  7. Regulation (emission standards, bans) is direct but inflexible — it works best when the externality is severe and measurement is straightforward.
  8. Elinor Ostrom showed that communities can govern commons successfully through self-organization — neither privatization nor government control is the only option.
  9. Sustainability requires accounting for externalities across time — the market cannot represent the interests of future generations.
  10. Climate change is the largest collective action problem humanity has ever faced — it combines global externalities, public goods, and commons governance at planetary scale.

docs.title: Think Like an Economist
docs.text:
Reflection Prompts

  1. Identify a negative externality you encounter in your daily life. Who bears the cost? Why does the market fail to account for it? What policy could address it?
  2. India's groundwater is a classic common pool resource. Using Ostrom's eight design principles, evaluate why community governance has succeeded in some Indian states (Rajasthan's johads) but not others (Punjab's tube wells). What institutional differences explain the divergent outcomes?
  3. A carbon tax makes fossil fuels more expensive, which disproportionately affects lower-income households who spend a larger share of their income on energy. Does this mean India should not implement a carbon tax? How might you design the policy to address this equity concern?

docs.title: Where to Go From Here
docs.text:
You have now completed all six modules of this course. You began with the foundational ideas of scarcity, opportunity cost, and trade-offs. You explored incentives and strategic behavior. You analyzed markets, labor, poverty, inequality, innovation, and growth. And you have ended here, with the recognition that markets — for all their power — have systematic blind spots when it comes to the environment, shared resources, and the future.

The economist's toolkit you have built is not a set of answers. It is a set of questions: What are the trade-offs? Who bears the costs? What incentives are driving behavior? Are the institutions well-designed? These questions apply to every policy debate you will encounter — from Delhi's air pollution to global climate negotiations, from local water management to international trade agreements.

Economics is not about memorizing models. It is about seeing the world clearly — with its trade-offs, its incentive structures, its winners and losers — and asking what we can do better. That is a skill that will serve you far beyond this course.

docs.title: Film Analysis: Erin Brockovich (2000)
docs.text: Director Steven Soderbergh Key Actors Julia Roberts, Albert Finney, Aaron Eckhart Genre Drama / Biography Runtime 131 minutes Setting Hinkley, California, 1993–1996 Module 6: Environmental and Public Economics

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
Erin Brockovich is an unemployed single mother of three who talks her way into a job as a legal assistant at a small law firm run by Ed Masry. While organizing files for a pro bono real estate case, she notices medical records mixed in with property documents — records that have no business being in a real estate file. Curious, she drives out to the small desert town of Hinkley, California, and begins talking to residents.

What she uncovers is devastating. Pacific Gas & Electric (PG&E), one of the largest utility companies in the United States, has been using hexavalent chromium — a known carcinogen — as a rust inhibitor at its Hinkley compressor station since the 1950s. The contaminated wastewater leached into the groundwater that Hinkley's residents drank, bathed in, and irrigated their gardens with. For decades, residents suffered unusually high rates of cancer, miscarriages, tumors, and chronic nosebleeds without understanding why. PG&E knew about the contamination and attempted to buy residents' silence through cheap land purchases.

Brockovich, who has no legal training and no scientific background, methodically documents the health records, water contamination data, and internal PG&E documents that prove the company knowingly poisoned a community. She organizes the 634 residents of Hinkley into a collective legal action against PG&E. The case results in a $333 million settlement — the largest direct-action lawsuit settlement in American history at the time. Brockovich receives a $2 million bonus.

The film is based on a true story, and the real Erin Brockovich continues to work as an environmental activist.

docs.title: Scene 1: Discovery of the Health Records
docs.text:
Economic Concepts: Information asymmetry, hidden externalities, market failure

Brockovich finds medical records tucked inside a real estate file — records that reveal PG&E offered to buy properties from residents while simultaneously concealing the health risks of contaminated groundwater. The residents did not know they were sick because of the water. PG&E did know.

This is a textbook case of information asymmetry: one party to a transaction possesses critical information that the other does not. PG&E's property buyout offers were priced to reflect the "clean" value of the land, not the contaminated reality. Residents, unaware that their water was poisoned, made decisions — to stay, to drink the water, to raise their children there — based on incomplete information. The market failed because the true cost of PG&E's industrial process was invisible to those who bore it.

What the Film Gets Right

The real PG&E did attempt to purchase contaminated properties without disclosing the contamination. Internal documents later revealed that the company had been aware of hexavalent chromium levels in groundwater far exceeding safety standards since the 1960s.

What the Film Simplifies

The film compresses the timeline and dramatizes the discovery. In reality, the connection between PG&E's operations and the contamination had been partially documented by regulatory agencies before Brockovich's involvement, but enforcement had been inadequate.

docs.title: Scene 2: Water Testing and Measuring the Damage
docs.text:
Economic Concepts: Measuring negative externalities, social cost, marginal damage

Brockovich collects water samples and sends them for testing. The results confirm hexavalent chromium levels far above safe limits. She then begins mapping the health consequences: cancers, reproductive disorders, immune deficiencies, clustered around the contamination plume.

This is the process of measuring a negative externality — quantifying the gap between the private cost of PG&E's operations (what the company paid for waste disposal, essentially zero since it dumped into unlined ponds) and the social cost (the health damage, medical expenses, reduced property values, and shortened lives of Hinkley residents). The difference between private cost and social cost is the externality, and it was enormous.

What the Film Gets Right

Hexavalent chromium is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer. The health effects depicted in the film — cancers, reproductive harm, respiratory damage — are consistent with documented chromium-6 exposure.

What the Film Simplifies

Establishing causation between contamination and specific health outcomes is scientifically complex. Epidemiological studies require large sample sizes and careful control for confounding factors. The film presents the link as more straightforward than it was in the actual legal proceedings.

docs.title: Scene 3: PG&E's Defense — Cost-Benefit from the Firm's Perspective
docs.text:
Economic Concepts: Private cost vs. social cost, cost-benefit analysis, externality as business strategy

When PG&E's lawyers confront Brockovich and Masry, the company's defense is implicitly economic: the contamination was an unintended byproduct of a legitimate industrial process, and the cost of properly disposing of the chromium waste would have been significantly higher than the cheap unlined ponds the company used. From PG&E's private cost-benefit calculation, the decision was rational — cheaper disposal meant lower operating costs, which meant higher profits.

This scene illustrates the core externality problem: when a firm's private cost calculation excludes the damage to third parties, the firm rationally chooses the socially destructive option. PG&E was not making an irrational decision. It was making a decision that the market's price signals — which excluded the health costs borne by Hinkley — encouraged.

What the Film Gets Right

The economic logic is accurate. Firms that can externalize costs have a competitive advantage over firms that internalize them. Without regulation or liability, the market rewards pollution.

What the Film Simplifies

The film portrays PG&E's behavior as straightforwardly villainous. The economic analysis is more nuanced: the absence of proper regulation, monitoring, and enforcement created the conditions that made this behavior privately rational. Changing the institutional environment — through stronger regulation or Pigouvian taxes — changes the firm's calculus.

docs.title: Scene 4: Organizing the Community — Collective Action
docs.text:
Economic Concepts: Free rider problem, collective action, transaction costs

Brockovich goes door to door in Hinkley, persuading 634 residents to join the lawsuit. This is harder than it sounds. Each resident faces a collective action problem: the lawsuit will be expensive, time-consuming, and emotionally draining. Any resident who stays out can still benefit if the case succeeds (PG&E may be forced to clean up the water regardless). The incentive to free ride — to let others bear the cost of litigation while enjoying the benefits — is strong.

Brockovich overcomes this through personal relationships, trust-building, and sheer persistence. She memorizes each family's story. She visits homes repeatedly. She becomes a member of the community rather than an outside expert. In economic terms, she reduces the transaction costs of organizing collective action and creates social capital — trust and reciprocity that makes cooperation possible.

What the Film Gets Right

Collective action problems in environmental litigation are real and severe. The real Erin Brockovich spent years building relationships with Hinkley residents. Her personal approach was critical to overcoming the distrust that corporate behavior and past legal disappointments had created.

What the Film Simplifies

The film focuses on Brockovich's personal heroism. In practice, the legal strategy — binding arbitration rather than a jury trial — was equally critical to the outcome, and the decision to pursue this route was made by the law firms involved.

docs.title: Scene 5: The Settlement — Regulatory vs. Legal Approaches
docs.text:
Economic Concepts: Litigation as externality correction, regulatory failure, property rights and liability

The case is settled through binding arbitration for $333 million — the largest direct-action settlement in US history at the time. The settlement forces PG&E to compensate victims for a damage that regulation had failed to prevent.

This outcome raises a fundamental question in environmental economics: should society rely on regulation (preventing harm before it occurs through emission standards and monitoring) or litigation (compensating victims after harm occurs through liability and lawsuits)? Regulation is proactive but requires enforcement capacity. Litigation is reactive but creates deterrence — if firms know they will be held liable, they have an incentive to prevent harm.

In Hinkley, regulation failed. California's Regional Water Quality Control Board had known about the contamination but had not forced adequate cleanup. The legal system — through the efforts of Brockovich and Masry — provided the accountability that the regulatory system did not.

docs.title: The Economics Behind the Story
docs.text:
Erin Brockovich is ultimately a story about what happens when the price system ignores social costs. PG&E's private cost of waste disposal was close to zero. The social cost — measured in cancers, deaths, and destroyed lives — was enormous. The gap between these two numbers is the externality, and for decades it went unpriced.

The film illustrates three responses to externalities: regulation (which failed in Hinkley because of inadequate enforcement), litigation (which eventually worked but only after decades of damage), and collective action (which Brockovich organized from the ground up). Each has strengths and limitations, and a well-designed policy system uses all three.

Indian Parallel

The Bhopal gas tragedy (1984) is the most devastating industrial externality in history and the closest Indian parallel to the Hinkley case — but at a vastly larger scale. When Union Carbide's pesticide plant leaked methyl isocyanate gas, between 3,800 and 16,000 people died (estimates vary), and over 500,000 were exposed to toxic gas. The parallels with Hinkley are striking: a multinational corporation externalizing costs onto a vulnerable community, regulatory failure (the factory operated with known safety deficiencies), information asymmetry (residents did not understand the risks), and inadequate compensation (the $470 million settlement in 1989 amounted to roughly $500 per victim).

But the differences are equally instructive. In Hinkley, the legal system eventually provided accountability. In Bhopal, legal proceedings dragged on for decades across Indian and American courts. Warren Anderson, Union Carbide's CEO, was charged with manslaughter by Indian courts but never extradited. The contaminated site has still not been fully cleaned up. The Bhopal case illustrates what happens when both regulation and litigation fail — and why institutional capacity for environmental governance is not a luxury but a necessity.

The Sterlite Copper smelter protests in Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu (2018) show that these issues remain active in India. Residents had protested for years against air and water pollution from the Vedanta-owned copper smelter. When protests escalated, police firing killed 13 people. The Tamil Nadu government subsequently ordered the smelter's permanent closure. The case raises the same economic questions as Erin Brockovich: who bears the external costs of industrial pollution, and what institutional mechanisms — regulation, litigation, or collective action — can hold polluters accountable?

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. PG&E's contamination was privately rational but socially destructive. Design a policy regime — using Pigouvian taxes, regulation, and liability rules — that would have prevented the Hinkley contamination. What trade-offs does your design create?
  2. Brockovich overcame the free rider problem through personal relationships and trust. Would this approach scale to a larger environmental problem — say, organizing residents across all of Delhi to demand clean air? What additional mechanisms would be needed?
  3. The Bhopal settlement of $470 million for over 500,000 victims has been called "the cheapest industrial disaster in history." Using the concept of externality pricing, discuss why courts and governments struggle to assign monetary values to health and life.
  4. Compare the regulatory environment in the Erin Brockovich case (1990s California) with the Sterlite case (2018 Tamil Nadu). What does the comparison suggest about the relationship between institutional capacity and environmental protection?
  5. The film ends with the settlement, but the real question is what happens next. Does a $333 million penalty actually deter future corporate pollution? Under what conditions does litigation succeed as a deterrent, and when does it fail?

docs.title: Further Viewing
docs.text:
• An Inconvenient Truth (2006) — Al Gore's documentary on climate change, framing carbon emissions as the largest negative externality in human history.
  • Dark Waters (2019) — A lawyer uncovers DuPont's decades-long contamination of a community's water supply with PFAS chemicals — a spiritual successor to Erin Brockovich with even more complex chemistry.
  • Kadvi Hawa (2017) — A Hindi film set in drought-stricken Bundelkhand, exploring how climate change and debt combine to destroy rural livelihoods. One of the rare Indian films that directly engages with environmental economics.
  • Minamata (2020) — Based on the real mercury poisoning disaster in Minamata, Japan, where a chemical factory externalized toxic waste onto a fishing community for decades.

docs.title: Nobel Focus: Elinor Ostrom
docs.text: Full Name Elinor Claire Ostrom (nee Awan) Born August 7, 1933, Los Angeles, California, USA Died June 12, 2012, Bloomington, Indiana, USA Nobel Prize 2009, Economic Sciences Field Institutional Analysis, Commons Governance, Political Economy Key Work Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action (1990)

docs.title: The Person
docs.text:
Elinor Ostrom grew up during the Great Depression in a working-class family in Los Angeles. Her mother, a seamstress, raised her largely alone. Neither parent had attended college, and in the 1950s, a woman pursuing a doctorate in political science was an anomaly. When she applied to the economics PhD program at UCLA, she was discouraged — a faculty member told her that women did not do well in the program. She enrolled in political science instead, a decision that would prove transformative: freed from the assumptions of orthodox economics, she developed an approach to studying institutions that was grounded in fieldwork and case studies rather than abstract mathematical modeling.

Her dissertation, on groundwater governance in Southern California, set the template for her life's work. Rather than modeling how water systems should be managed in theory, she studied how communities actually managed them in practice. She discovered that Los Angeles-area water users had developed complex, self-organized institutions to allocate groundwater — and that these institutions often worked better than the state-imposed alternatives that experts recommended.

In 1965, she joined Indiana University in Bloomington, where she spent the rest of her career. With her husband Vincent Ostrom, she founded the Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis — a deliberately interdisciplinary center that brought together economists, political scientists, anthropologists, ecologists, and practitioners to study how real communities govern shared resources.

For decades, her work was largely ignored by mainstream economists, who saw commons governance as a solved problem: Hardin's "Tragedy of the Commons" said shared resources would be depleted unless privatized or regulated, and that was that. Ostrom's patient accumulation of counter-evidence — case after case of communities that had successfully governed commons for centuries — gradually made the argument impossible to dismiss.

In 2009, she became the first woman to receive the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. She shared it with Oliver Williamson "for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons." She was 76 years old. She died three years later, in 2012.

docs.title: The Contribution
docs.text:
Ostrom's central insight was both simple and radical: the choice between privatization and government regulation is a false binary. There is a third option — community self-governance — and it has been working, in many places, for a very long time.

The starting point for her critique was Garrett Hardin's 1968 "Tragedy of the Commons." Hardin argued that any shared resource open to all users will inevitably be destroyed, because each user has an incentive to take as much as possible. The metaphor was a village pasture: each herder adds more cattle because the benefit is private but the overgrazing cost is shared. The only solutions, Hardin concluded, were privatization or state control.

Ostrom's response was empirical, not theoretical. She did not argue that the Tragedy was logically wrong. She argued that it was empirically incomplete. By studying hundreds of real-world commons — fisheries in Maine and Turkey, irrigation systems in Nepal and Spain, forests in Japan and India, pastures in Switzerland and East Africa — she found that many communities had successfully governed shared resources for generations, sometimes centuries, without either privatization or external regulation.

What distinguished successful commons from failed ones? Ostrom identified eight design principles that appeared consistently in durable, well-managed commons:

  1. Clearly defined boundaries — The resource and its users are clearly delineated. You cannot manage a commons if you do not know who is in and who is out.
  2. Congruence between rules and local conditions — Harvesting rules are adapted to the specific ecology, economy, and culture of the place. One-size-fits-all rules imposed from outside typically fail.
  3. Collective-choice arrangements — The people affected by the rules participate in creating and modifying them. Rules imposed by outsiders lack legitimacy and local knowledge.
  4. Monitoring — Compliance is observed by the users themselves or by agents accountable to the users, not by distant bureaucrats.
  5. Graduated sanctions — First-time violators receive mild penalties; repeat offenders face escalating consequences. This allows for honest mistakes while deterring deliberate exploitation.
  6. Conflict-resolution mechanisms — Disputes are resolved quickly and locally, without expensive litigation.
  7. Minimal recognition of rights to organize — External authorities (governments) do not undermine the community's right to create and enforce its own rules.
  8. Nested enterprises — For large-scale resources, governance is organized in multiple layers — from local to regional to national — with each level handling decisions at the appropriate scale.

The Key Insight

Hardin assumed that commons users were trapped in a prisoner's dilemma — each rational individual would overuse the resource because they could not trust others to restrain themselves. Ostrom showed that when communities can communicate, build trust, create rules, and enforce them, they escape the dilemma. The tragedy of the commons is not inevitable; it is a consequence of institutional failure, not human nature.

docs.title: Why It Matters Today
docs.text:
Ostrom's framework is more relevant now than when she first proposed it. Climate change, biodiversity loss, ocean acidification, and groundwater depletion are all commons problems at varying scales. International climate negotiations — from Kyoto to Paris — are attempts at governing the global atmospheric commons, and they exhibit many of the challenges Ostrom studied: defining boundaries, creating rules, monitoring compliance, and sanctioning free riders.

Her work also provides a counterweight to the assumption that environmental problems require either markets (carbon trading, property rights) or governments (regulation, taxation) alone. In practice, the most effective environmental governance often involves all three: community management at the local level, government regulation at the regional level, and market mechanisms at the national or international level — precisely the "nested enterprises" she described.

In India

India is arguably the richest laboratory for Ostrom's ideas in the world, with centuries-old traditions of community resource management alongside modern challenges of institutional erosion.

  • Van Panchayats in Uttarakhand: These community forest councils, formalized in 1931 but rooted in much older practices, manage over 500,000 hectares of forest across roughly 12,000 villages. Each Van Panchayat sets harvesting rules, monitors compliance, and imposes penalties — a near-perfect instantiation of Ostrom's design principles. Research by Agrawal (2005) and Agrawal and Ostrom (2001) found that community-managed forests often maintained better tree cover and biodiversity than adjacent state-managed forests.

  • Joint Forest Management (JFM): Launched in 1990, India's JFM program creates partnerships between state forest departments and local communities to manage degraded forests. Over 100,000 JFM committees manage roughly 22 million hectares. The program's mixed record — successful in some states, ineffective in others — maps directly onto Ostrom's framework: success correlates with genuine community participation in rule-making (principle 3), local monitoring (principle 4), and government recognition of community authority (principle 7).

  • Traditional water harvesting in Rajasthan: The johads (earthen check dams), baoris (stepwells), and tankas (underground cisterns) of Rajasthan are physical infrastructure for commons governance. Revived by Rajendra Singh's Tarun Bharat Sangh from the 1980s onward, these systems recharged groundwater, restored rivers, and rebuilt rural economies — all through collective action organized at the village level.

  • Fishing communities in Kerala: Traditional fishing communities along Kerala's coast have governed marine commons through informal institutions called koodams (assemblies) for generations. These bodies regulate fishing seasons, restrict destructive gear types, and allocate fishing grounds — all without formal legal authority. Their effectiveness illustrates Ostrom's point that communities can manage even mobile, hard-to-monitor resources when the institutional architecture is sound.

  • Tank irrigation in Tamil Nadu: Thousands of traditional irrigation tanks (eris) in Tamil Nadu were historically managed by village communities under customary rules governing water allocation, maintenance obligations, and conflict resolution. Colonial and post-colonial centralization weakened these institutions, and many tanks fell into disrepair — a cautionary example of what happens when principle 7 (external recognition of self-governance) is violated.

docs.title: Connection to Erin Brockovich
docs.text:
At first glance, Erin Brockovich seems like the opposite of an Ostrom story: it is about a community that failed to protect its commons (groundwater) and had to rely on the legal system for redress. But look more closely, and Ostrom's framework illuminates the case.

The residents of Hinkley lacked almost all of Ostrom's design principles: they had no collective-choice institution, no monitoring system, no mechanism for detecting or sanctioning PG&E's contamination. They did not even know the resource was being degraded. What Brockovich created — by going door to door, building trust, sharing information, and organizing 634 residents into a collective legal action — was, in essence, an Ostrom-style commons institution, improvised from scratch to solve a specific governance failure.

The contrast is instructive. Where Ostrom's communities governed commons proactively — building institutions before the crisis — Hinkley's residents had to organize reactively, after decades of damage. Both stories underscore the same lesson: collective action is the foundation of commons governance, whether it takes the form of a centuries-old Van Panchayat or a lawsuit organized by a single determined individual.

docs.text:
1. Ostrom, E. (1990). Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action. Cambridge University Press. DOI: 10.1017/CBO9780511807763 — The foundational work laying out the eight design principles and the evidence from case studies worldwide.
  2. Ostrom, E. (2005). Understanding Institutional Diversity. Princeton University Press. — Develops the Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework for studying how rules shape resource governance.
  3. Ostrom, E., Burger, J., Field, C. B., Norgaard, R. B., & Policansky, D. (1999). "Revisiting the Commons: Local Lessons, Global Challenges." Science, 284(5412), 278-282. DOI: 10.1126/science.284.5412.278

docs.title: Module 6 Quiz: Environmental and Public Economics
docs.text: Test your understanding of the key concepts from Module 6. Each question has one correct answer. Click "Show Answer" to check your response.

docs.title: 1. A factory discharges effluent into a river, damaging fisheries downstream. The factory's owners and customers do not bear this cost. This is an example of:
docs.text:
1. A positive externality
  2. A negative externality
  3. A public good
  4. A Pigouvian tax
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A negative externality is a cost imposed on third parties who are not part of the transaction. The factory and its customers benefit from cheap production, but the downstream fishing communities bear the pollution cost without compensation. The market price of the factory's product does not reflect this social cost, so the market overproduces relative to the socially optimal level.

Concept Tested: Negative Externality

docs.title: 2. India's pulse polio immunization campaign, which vaccinated hundreds of millions of children and achieved polio-free status in 2014, is an example of addressing which economic problem?
docs.text:
1. The free rider problem in public goods
  2. Underproduction due to a positive externality
  3. The tragedy of the commons
  4. Moral hazard in healthcare
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Vaccination generates a positive externality: each vaccinated child protects not only themselves but everyone they might have infected (herd immunity). Because the social benefit exceeds the private benefit, the market alone would produce too few vaccinations. Government subsidy and provision push vaccination closer to the socially optimal level.

Concept Tested: Positive Externality

docs.title: 3. National defense is the classic example of a public good because it is:
docs.text:
1. Expensive and requires government funding
  2. Non-rival and non-excludable
  3. Rival and excludable
  4. Provided by the private sector through competition
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A public good has two defining features: it is non-rival (one person's consumption does not reduce availability for others — defending one citizen does not reduce defense for another) and non-excludable (you cannot prevent any resident from benefiting). Cost (A) is not the defining feature — many expensive goods are private. The non-rival, non-excludable combination is what creates the free rider problem that makes private provision inadequate.

Concept Tested: Public Good

docs.title: 4. India is the world's largest user of groundwater, with over 30 million tube wells and minimal extraction regulation. Each farmer pumps as much as possible before neighbors drain the aquifer. This situation best illustrates:
docs.text:
1. A positive externality
  2. The free rider problem
  3. The tragedy of the commons
  4. Cap-and-trade failure
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Groundwater is a common pool resource — rival (water pumped by one farmer is unavailable to others) but non-excludable (enforcement of extraction limits is nearly impossible with millions of users). Each farmer has an incentive to extract as much as possible, depleting the shared aquifer. This is the classic Tragedy of the Commons: individually rational behavior leads to collective resource destruction.

Concept Tested: Tragedy of the Commons

docs.title: 5. A Pigouvian tax on carbon emissions works by:
docs.text:
1. Banning the use of fossil fuels above a certain threshold
  2. Giving firms free permits to pollute up to a set limit
  3. Making polluters pay the social cost of their emissions, so the market price reflects the true cost
  4. Subsidizing firms that use renewable energy
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A Pigouvian tax is set equal to the external cost per unit of the harmful activity. By forcing polluters to pay the social cost, the tax raises the market price of carbon-intensive goods, reducing demand and production to a level closer to the social optimum. It uses the price mechanism rather than fighting it — polluters choose how to reduce emissions (cleaner technology, less output, fuel switching), and the market finds the cheapest path. A ban (A) is command-and-control regulation. Free permits (B) describe cap-and-trade. Subsidies (D) are a different policy tool.

Concept Tested: Pigouvian Tax

docs.title: 6. Under a cap-and-trade system, which of the following is TRUE?
docs.text:
1. The government sets the price of pollution and lets firms choose how much to pollute
  2. The government sets the total quantity of pollution and lets the market determine the price of permits
  3. Firms are free to pollute without limit as long as they purchase permits
  4. The system works only if all firms face the same cost of reducing pollution
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Under cap-and-trade, the government sets a cap on total emissions and issues permits up to that amount. Firms that can reduce emissions cheaply sell their excess permits to firms that find reduction more expensive. The permit price is determined by supply and demand in the permit market. This achieves the environmental target at the lowest possible total cost. Option A describes a tax (price-based) rather than cap-and-trade (quantity-based). Option C is wrong because the total quantity is capped. Option D is wrong — the system works precisely because firms have different abatement costs, allowing gains from trade.

Concept Tested: Cap-and-Trade

docs.title: 7. In Erin Brockovich, PG&E contaminated Hinkley's groundwater with hexavalent chromium for decades. Residents did not know their water was poisoned. This is an example of:
docs.text:
1. The tragedy of the commons
  2. A Pigouvian tax failure
  3. Information asymmetry combined with a negative externality
  4. The free rider problem
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. PG&E possessed information about the contamination that residents did not — a classic information asymmetry. The contamination itself was a negative externality: PG&E's industrial process imposed health costs on residents who were not party to the company's production decisions. The combination is especially harmful: the externality was invisible to those bearing the cost, which prevented them from taking protective action or demanding accountability.

Concept Tested: Externalities / Information Asymmetry (Film Connection)

docs.title: 8. Elinor Ostrom's research showed that the Tragedy of the Commons is NOT inevitable when communities:
docs.text:
1. Privatize the resource and assign individual property rights
  2. Wait for government regulation to impose extraction limits
  3. Develop self-governing institutions with clear rules, monitoring, and graduated sanctions
  4. Abandon the shared resource and find alternatives
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Ostrom's central finding was that communities can successfully govern shared resources through self-organization — without privatization (A) or top-down government regulation (B). Her eight design principles — including clear boundaries, locally adapted rules, collective choice, monitoring by users, and graduated sanctions — describe the institutional features that distinguish successful commons from failed ones. Abandoning the resource (D) is not governance; it is retreat.

Concept Tested: Commons Governance / Ostrom's Design Principles (Nobel Connection)

docs.title: 9. Uttarakhand's Van Panchayats — community-managed forest councils dating back to the 1930s — are considered a real-world validation of Ostrom's theory because they:
docs.text:
1. Were imposed by the British colonial government as a top-down regulation
  2. Privatized forest land by giving individual villagers ownership of specific plots
  3. Feature community-made rules, local monitoring, and graduated penalties — matching Ostrom's design principles
  4. Rely on the state forest department for all enforcement
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Van Panchayats are community-governed institutions where village councils set harvesting rules, community members monitor compliance, and violators face graduated penalties — closely matching Ostrom's eight design principles. While formalized under British-era Van Panchayat Rules of 1931, they are rooted in older community practices. Research by Agrawal and Ostrom (2001) found that these community-managed forests often achieved better ecological outcomes than either state-managed forests or open-access areas.

Concept Tested: Ostrom's Design Principles / Indian Application

docs.title: 10. Climate change is described as "the largest collective action problem humanity has ever faced." This is because:
docs.text:
1. Climate science is uncertain and economists cannot model the problem
  2. Carbon emissions are a global negative externality, the atmosphere is a commons, and each nation has an incentive to free ride on others' mitigation efforts
  3. Climate change only affects developing countries, so wealthy nations have no incentive to act
  4. The technology to address climate change does not yet exist
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Climate change combines every market failure concept in this module. Carbon emissions are a negative externality at global scale — each emitter imposes costs on the entire planet. The atmosphere is a global common pool resource. Climate stability is a public good — non-rival and non-excludable. And each nation faces a free rider incentive: the cost of reducing emissions is borne domestically, while the benefit is shared globally. This creates a collective action problem of unprecedented scale and complexity.

Concept Tested: Collective Action / Externalities / Public Goods / Sustainability

These browser-based simulations are from Dan McCreary's Introduction to Economics open textbook, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. They run entirely in your browser --- no installation or login required.

Each simulation lets you adjust inputs and observe how economic models respond. They are organized below by the course module they most closely support. Click any link to open the simulation in a new tab.

docs.title: Module 1: Understanding Economic Thinking
docs.text:
Scarcity, opportunity cost, trade-offs, economic systems, and thinking like an economist.

Simulation What It Teaches Link Opportunity Cost Calculator Quantifies the trade-offs involved in choosing one option over another Open PPF Explorer Visualizes the production possibilities frontier and efficient vs. inefficient allocations Open Economic Systems Spectrum Compares market, command, mixed, and traditional economic systems on a spectrum Open Correlation vs. Causation Demonstrates why correlation does not imply causation with interactive examples Open

docs.title: Module 2: Incentives and Human Behavior
docs.text:
Demand, utility, budget constraints, elasticity, and behavioral responses to incentives.

Simulation What It Teaches Link Demand Curve Explorer Shows how price changes affect quantity demanded along a demand curve Open Marginal Utility Meter Illustrates diminishing marginal utility as consumption increases Open Budget Constraint Explorer Visualizes how income and prices determine the set of affordable choices Open Elasticity Calculator Computes price elasticity of demand and shows elastic vs. inelastic responses Open Diminishing Marginal Benefit Shows how additional units of a good provide progressively less benefit Open

docs.title: Module 3: Market Dynamics and Labor Markets
docs.text:
Supply, demand, equilibrium, market structures, price controls, and labor markets.

Simulation What It Teaches Link Supply and Demand Interactive supply and demand diagram with shifting curves and equilibrium Open Market Equilibrium Explorer Shows how markets reach equilibrium through price adjustment Open Market Structure Spectrum Compares perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, and monopoly Open Price Ceiling Simulator Demonstrates the effects of price ceilings, including shortages Open Price Floor Visualizer Demonstrates the effects of price floors, including surpluses Open Labor Force Breakdown Breaks down the population into employed, unemployed, and not in labor force Open Unemployment Classifier Classifies types of unemployment: frictional, structural, and cyclical Open

docs.title: Module 4: Poverty, Inequality, and Development
docs.text:
GDP measurement, efficiency vs. equity, human capital, and development indicators.

Simulation What It Teaches Link GDP Calculator Computes GDP using the expenditure approach (C + I + G + NX) Open GDP Components Breakdown Visualizes the relative shares of consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports Open Efficiency-Equity Spectrum Explores the trade-off between economic efficiency and equitable distribution Open Human Capital ROI Calculator Estimates the return on investment in education and skills Open

docs.title: Module 5: Innovation, Technology, and Growth
docs.text:
Network effects, platform economics, compound growth, nominal vs. real values, and the attention economy.

Simulation What It Teaches Link Network Effects Visualizer Shows how the value of a product increases as more people use it Open Platform Economics Simulator Models two-sided markets where platforms connect buyers and sellers Open Compound Interest Visualizer Demonstrates the power of compound growth over time Open Nominal vs. Real GDP Illustrates the difference between nominal and inflation-adjusted GDP Open Attention Economy Explores how attention is a scarce resource in digital markets Open

docs.title: Module 6: Environmental and Public Economics
docs.text:
Externalities, public goods, commons, taxation, and policy evaluation.

Simulation What It Teaches Link Negative Externality Visualizer Shows how negative externalities cause markets to overproduce harmful goods Open Public Goods Game Simulates the free-rider problem in public goods provision Open Tragedy of the Commons Models how shared resources are depleted when individuals act in self-interest Open Tax Incidence Explorer Shows how the burden of a tax is shared between buyers and sellers depending on elasticities Open Policy Claim Evaluator Helps evaluate the logic and evidence behind common economic policy claims Open Feedback Loops Visualizes positive and negative feedback loops in economic systems Open

Attribution

All simulations are from Dan McCreary's Introduction to Economics, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

docs.title: Economist Stories
docs.text:
These biographical narratives are from Dan McCreary's Introduction to Economics open textbook, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Each story provides an accessible introduction to the life, context, and key contributions of an influential economist.

The stories are organized below by the course module they most closely support. Several economists are relevant to more than one module --- their primary placement reflects the strongest thematic fit.

docs.title: Module 1: Understanding Economic Thinking
docs.text:
Foundations of economic thought, scarcity, trade, and the origins of the discipline.

Economist Key Insight Link Adam Smith Division of labor, the invisible hand, and the foundations of market economics Read Ibn Khaldun Pioneering analysis of supply, demand, taxation, and economic cycles centuries before Smith Read Harriet Martineau Made classical economics accessible to the public through narrative and illustration Read Thomas Sowell Applied basic economic reasoning --- incentives, trade-offs, prices --- to public policy debates Read

docs.title: Module 2: Incentives and Human Behavior
docs.text:
Markets, planning, strategic behavior, and the role of information.

Economist Key Insight Link Friedrich Hayek The price system as a mechanism for coordinating dispersed knowledge; the limits of central planning Read John Maynard Keynes Aggregate demand, animal spirits, and the case for government intervention during recessions Read

docs.title: Module 3: Market Dynamics and Labor Markets
docs.text:
Labor markets, monetary policy, and the macroeconomy.

Economist Key Insight Link Janet Yellen Labor market dynamics, the Federal Reserve, and navigating monetary policy through crises Read

docs.title: Module 4: Poverty, Inequality, and Development
docs.text:
Capabilities, microfinance, experimental methods, and structural inequality.

Economist Key Insight Link Amartya Sen The capability approach to welfare, famine as a failure of entitlements, and development as freedom Read Muhammad Yunus Microcredit and the Grameen Bank --- banking for the poor as a tool for development Read Esther Duflo Randomized controlled trials in development economics --- testing what works with evidence Read W.E.B. Du Bois Pioneered the empirical study of racial economic inequality in America Read Acemoglu & Robinson Why institutions --- not geography or culture --- are the fundamental cause of long-run development Read Lisa Cook Documented how violence and discrimination suppressed African American innovation and patenting Read

docs.title: Module 5: Innovation, Technology, and Growth
docs.text:
Innovation, patents, and the economics of knowledge.

Economist Key Insight Link Lisa Cook How barriers to innovation --- including racial violence --- reduce technological progress and growth Read

docs.title: Module 6: Environmental and Public Economics
docs.text:
Commons governance, environmental sustainability, and collective action.

Economist Key Insight Link Elinor Ostrom Communities can govern shared resources without privatization or top-down regulation Read Wangari Maathai Linked environmental sustainability with women's empowerment and grassroots economic development Read

Attribution

All Economist Stories are from Dan McCreary's Introduction to Economics, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
